json.title: Feature request: `bad_data: dead-letter` mode for Kafka sources (retain undecodable records in a DLQ topic)
json.body:
## Problem

Arroyo Kafka sources support `bad_data: fail | drop`. `fail` makes a single poisoned record fatal to the whole pipeline (we measured a 27h outage from one bad magic byte). `drop` protects availability but discards the payload — the record is only visible as a counter in deserialization error metrics. There is no built-in way to *retain* the undecodable bytes for later inspection / replay.

Operators are left choosing between availability and forensics. Kafka ecosystems solved this long ago with dead-letter queues (Kafka Connect `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name`, Flink side outputs, etc.).

## Proposal

A third `bad_data` mode on Kafka sources:

```sql
CREATE TABLE src (...) WITH (
  connector = 'kafka',
  type = 'source',
  'bad_data' = 'dead-letter',
  'bad_data.dead_letter.topic' = 'my.dlq'
);
```

Semantics: on deserialization failure, produce the ORIGINAL raw bytes to the configured topic with provenance headers (`source_topic`, `source_partition`, `source_offset`, `source_timestamp`, `error`), count it (same metric as `drop`), and continue. Delivery to the DLQ should be at-least-once; a DLQ produce failure should surface as a source error (configurable: warn vs fail).

## Why upstream (and not only a side consumer)

We currently deploy an external "sweeper" that re-validates the same topics and copies undecodable records to a DLQ. It works, but:
- it duplicates the deserialization work on every record of every topic;
- its drop decision can drift from the engine's (schema registry cache timing, decoder version skew);
- the engine already holds the failing bytes at the exact failure point — emitting them is the cheapest correct implementation.

## Notes

- Applies to any self-describing wire format source (avro+SR, json schema).
- A per-source override of the DLQ topic matters (multi-tenant platforms route by domain).
- Happy to contribute the implementation if the design direction is acceptable to the maintainers.

The 27h outage from a single poisoned record and the external sweeper workaround really stood out here.

We’ve been working on the operator-side of this recovery problem with ReplayGuard.

ReplayGuard doesn’t replace the need to capture the undecodable record into a DLQ — but once failed records are retained, we provide a controlled recovery workflow around selecting the recovery scope, validating/dry-running it, redriving with rate controls, pause/resume/stop, and keeping an audit trail.

Your point about preserving the original record for later inspection/replay is very aligned with what we’re seeing in production recovery workflows.

If you’re open to it, would you be interested in a short 15–20 min discussion? I’d really like to understand the operator workflow you want after dead-lettering and compare it with what we’ve built.

https://replayguard.in
